profile.name: Filip Heinel
profile.headline: Full-stack developer, problem solver, organiser and planner, and a bridge between tech, business and, most importantly, users. Five years of TypeScript, React, Next.js and Node, most recently as a consultant for Affärsvärlden and Suntarbetsliv. Now SEO and development at Emax Media.

suntarbetsliv.title: Friskfaktorlabbet for Suntarbetsliv
suntarbetsliv.oneLiner: A reusable form tool that guides work groups through improving their health factors, built over two years as a consultant through Kumpan, with the project management around it.
suntarbetsliv.problem: Suntarbetsliv is run jointly by unions and employer organisations, for people who work in municipalities and regions. Friskfaktorlabbet gives a manager and a safety representative guided activities to run with their work group: everyone rates the workplace's health factors, then the group agrees on where things stand, prioritises and makes a plan. The tool had to carry several activities like that, not one fixed form.
constraints: I took over a legacy, custom-built WordPress setup at short notice, with a tight deadline.
Suntarbetsliv's site was still on WordPress, so the tool had to live there.
It had to stay maintainable after the contract, by Suntarbetsliv or the next team.
About ten people were involved around it, so plans and priorities had to stay clear.
suntarbetsliv.role: I worked in a core team of four, with one other developer, and about ten people around us. I built the tool full-stack, shaped its architecture and took on nearly all the project management on the assignment. Later I worked in Next.js, Payload and Supabase too, and built the AI chatbot on suntarbetsliv.se, using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and vector search.

decisions.name: One reusable tool, not one-off forms
decisions.line: The activities are built from reusable components, so a new one doesn't mean starting over.

decisions.name: WordPress, for now
decisions.line: Suntarbetsliv hadn't moved off WordPress yet, so the tool was built in PHP and MySQL, inside the site they already had.

decisions.name: Take the reins, work Lean
decisions.line: With a tight deadline on a build that was new to me, I took the reins and ran the work the Lean startup way: small, fast steps, each checked against what the client and the users needed. That kept the other developer and me in close step too.

decisions.name: A chatbot with a feedback loop
decisions.line: The chatbot uses RAG: it finds relevant material with vector search in pgvector before it answers. Every answer was logged and could be rated or flagged, which gave a feedback loop for improving it.

suntarbetsliv.result: We met the deadline with a tool that fit the client and its users, and Friskfaktorlabbet is live today.

ai-skills.title: AI skills, maintained like software
ai-skills.oneLiner: A personal Claude plugin: 14 researched methods as skills, tested and maintained by subagents and a scheduled agent run. It's built like software, with CI on every push, a cost budget, versioned releases and an export to five other AI agent clients.
ai-skills.problem: AI assistants answer confidently, even when they're wrong, and good method gets lost between chats and projects. That means answers someone has to check again, and results that depend on who asked and how. I wanted the methods I rely on to be explicit, sourced and applied the same way every time, without the cost of loading them growing out of hand.
constraints: Every skill's description loads into every conversation, so each one costs tokens all the time.
The agents read web pages and GitHub issues, and outside text can carry instructions meant to hijack them.
No private names may reach a skill.
Dated facts and links go stale, so they need rechecking at the source.
It has to work in other AI clients too, not only in Claude.
ai-skills.role: My own project. I research and write the methods, and designed how the plugin is built, tested and maintained. I built the test, measurement and release tooling in Python and GitHub Actions, set up the agent workflows around it, and approve every release.

agentic.name: A routing eval, run by a subagent
agentic.line: In every maintenance run, a read-only subagent on a smaller model sees only each skill's name and description, and picks a skill for each of 54 example requests. A wrong pick points to the description that misled it.

agentic.name: Three reviewers, one brief
agentic.line: Before the latest release, three read-only subagents each reviewed a part of the plugin against the same brief, looking for anything tied to one project or person. Their findings became one plan, and I decided what changed.

agentic.name: A scheduled maintenance agent
agentic.line: Every quarter, an agent run measures the plugin, rechecks dated facts and links at their sources, works through lessons logged as GitHub issues and opens a draft pull request with a report. Nothing merges until I approve it.

agentic.name: From chat to issue to release
agentic.line: A correction in any chat becomes a GitHub issue, one per lesson, so chats running at the same time never overwrite each other. The maintenance run turns them into changes, and only it closes them.

agentic.name: The right model for each step
agentic.line: Helpers that check, review or fetch run on a smaller, cheaper model. The model-choice skill, built on research into model routing and cascades such as FrugalGPT and RouteLLM, applies the same rule to any task: cheap checks first, and a larger model only when a check fails.

agentic.name: Guarded against prompt injection
agentic.line: Text from web pages and issues counts as data, never as instructions, and the helpers that read it can't change anything. The security skill also reviews AI agent setups against OWASP's Top 10 lists for LLM and agentic applications.

skills.name: Source evaluation
skills.line: A 1–5 trust score per claim, built on the Swedish Psychological Defence Agency's “Kolla källan” questions. It scores what a rule says separately from what people actually do.

skills.name: Decision analysis
skills.line: Multi-criteria scoring with swing weights. People weigh independently, so the first speaker doesn't anchor everyone. A robustness check runs across hundreds of nearby weightings, and the process ends with a pre-mortem.

skills.name: Estimates
skills.line: Time, cost and usage as a range with a P50 and a P80: how similar cases went first, then a simulation of the parts, then a check against what actually happened.

skills.name: UX and UI
skills.line: 16 principles drawn from Nielsen Norman Group, GOV.UK and Apple's and Google's design guidelines, with a screenshot review checklist.

skills.name: Accessibility
skills.line: WCAG 2.2 AA in practice, tested with axe-core plus a keyboard and screen-reader pass.

skills.name: Plain writing
skills.line: The plain-language standard ISO 24495-1, applied with Swedish klarspråk and plain English: the most important thing first, one idea per sentence, common words.

skills.name: Data modelling
skills.line: Cardinality, keeping data consistent where there are no transactions, concurrency, versioned migrations, and Postgres/Supabase row-level security.

skills.name: Security review
skills.line: A threat model with STRIDE, then checks against the OWASP Top 10 and ASVS for web apps, repositories, CI and AI agents. A review aid, not a penetration test.

skills.name: Plugin engineering
skills.line: Lessons from building and running plugins, especially ones a team shares: what works, what breaks, and the checks that prevent it.

skills.name: Model choice
skills.line: Which model and effort level for each step: cheap checks first, and a larger model only when a check fails. Written for any AI client and for self-hosted models.

skills.name: Maintenance
skills.line: Upkeep of this plugin: measuring its token use, testing which skill each request picks, rechecking facts and links, working through logged lessons, and building new versions.

skills.name: Lesson intake
skills.line: Corrections and findings from any chat become GitHub issues: made general, checked for duplicates, and filed only after the user says yes.

skills.name: Proactive help
skills.line: After the answer, at most three suggestions tied to the user's own plans: collisions, closing windows, single points of failure and missing steps. Nothing is done without a yes.

skills.name: What I need from you
skills.line: Every reply that needs an answer or an action from the user ends with one numbered list of questions and actions, with labels that carry over until each one is answered or done.

ai-skills.origin: Most of these methods started in my planning platform, a side project with a trip planner, and an event planner to follow. There they keep the data model, the accessibility tests and the fact-checking consistent.

decisions.name: Treat skills as software
decisions.line: The source lives in GitHub, and every push runs CI in GitHub Actions: the self-test, the export and the cost measurement. The self-test checks structure, versions, references and valid frontmatter, and blocks private names, which it knows only as salted hashes.

decisions.name: Evidence first
decisions.line: Ten of the skills rest on cited research, standards and official guidance, with every source scored 1–5. Before a fact is stored, shared or relied on, Claude checks it at the original source, looks harder at anything implausible and marks what it couldn't confirm.

decisions.name: Checked from outside
decisions.line: Research shows models are poor at catching their own mistakes without outside feedback. So the checks run against sources, tests and separate reviewers rather than the model's own opinion, and I approve anything that matters. That lowers the risk of made-up facts; it doesn't remove it.

decisions.name: A budget for cost
decisions.line: A script estimates tokens in three tiers: descriptions, loaded in every chat; instructions, loaded when a skill is used; and reference files, loaded only when read. The self-test fails if the descriptions together pass about 1,500 tokens.

decisions.name: Portable, not locked in
decisions.line: An export packages the skills in the open Agent Skills format, with an install guide for Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot and OpenCode. Claude-only features are marked, each with a fallback for other clients.

decisions.name: Release from clean source
decisions.line: Every build gets a version bump and a changelog entry. A release script checks the packaged files against the source and keeps every version with checksums.

value.name: Lower running cost
value.line: What loads in every conversation is measured and capped, and the checking runs on cheaper models.

value.name: Answers you can check
value.line: Facts trace back to scored sources, and anything that couldn't be confirmed is marked as such.

value.name: Change without surprises
value.line: Every change passes the tests and my review before it merges, and ships as a versioned release with a changelog.

value.name: Risk kept in check
value.line: A person approves anything that matters, private names can't get in, and outside text is treated as data, which makes the agents harder to hijack.

value.name: No lock-in
value.line: The same skills install in six AI agent clients, Claude among them.

ai-skills.result: Fourteen skills, in daily use across my own projects. The part loaded in every conversation comes to about 1,170 tokens, down from about 1,320 before the latest release, even with a skill added.

delivery.title: Delivery system for AI-assisted client work
delivery.oneLiner: The controls around an AI-assisted workflow for client documents: figures you can trace, a person approving anything a client sees, and lessons from live work reviewed before they change the method.
delivery.problem: Client work has to be consistent and safe to show, but one specialist's judgment is hard to repeat across many clients.
constraints: Client data and decisions must never move from one account to another.
Every figure in a client document has to trace back to a source and a period.
Nothing reaches a client without a person's yes.
The work has to carry on when the AI tool is down.
delivery.role: I designed the operating layer around an AI-assisted workflow for client documents: the rules, the checks and the fallback. I designed it on my own. The professional rules in it build on what experienced colleagues have learned, and on their feedback.

decisions.name: Three layers, kept apart
decisions.line: Shared professional standards, my own preferences and one client's decisions each live in their own place, so one client's choice never becomes everyone's rule.

decisions.name: Labelled by audience
decisions.line: Every draft says who it's for, so internal notes stay internal.

decisions.name: Improve on a schedule
decisions.line: The method changes on a cadence, not on impulse. Corrections wait for a scheduled review.

decisions.name: A written fallback
decisions.line: A written method describes how the work continues when the AI tool is unavailable.

steps.name: Export
steps.line: Data comes in as exports from several tools, and exports are messy.

steps.name: Check
steps.line: Every figure gets a source and a period. A file that can't be read is reported, never skipped.

steps.name: Reconcile
steps.line: Where two tools disagree, it is settled before anything is written.

steps.name: Draft
steps.line: A first draft is written with AI assistance, within the shared standards and that client's own decisions, and labelled by audience.

steps.name: Approve
steps.line: I review every draft. Nothing reaches the client or a shared folder without my clear yes.

steps.name: Learn
steps.line: Corrections are sorted as personal, one account or general. General ones wait for the scheduled review.

delivery.boundary: Built for real client work. No client material, tool names or internal methods are shown here.

nether.title: Nether
nether.oneLiner: A discretion-first community built around events in the cities you choose: contact on your terms, trust that members earn from each other, and every safety tool free.
premise: Dating apps and niche community platforms leave a lot of room to do better. Safety often falls on whoever gets contacted, and the tools that keep people safe often cost extra. Nether starts with gender, sexuality and relationship minorities in Sweden, and is meant to work for everyone else too.

Nether is my attempt to change that. Safety comes in layers: consent before contact, visibility each person controls, and members who can vouch for each other. The business model has to pay for running and moderating a safe platform, without tricks that work against the people using it.

And it's made for people, not users. Each person decides how visible they are, what contact they accept, which cities they follow and how much of themselves they show, and it works fully for people who never show their face.
Some apps and communities already get parts of this right, and I'd rather build on that with them than compete.
nether.role: My own project. I designed and built it on my own.
constraints: Contact follows rules each member sets, and only members who opt in appear in the card stack.
Explicit photos have to stay hidden from anyone who hasn't chosen to see them.
Hosting has to be in the EU.

decisions.name: No swipe deck, no open forum
decisions.line: Matching is an opt-in list of cards with Like and Pass, not a swipe gesture. Instead of an open forum there are a few moderated boards, for a place or an interest, where trial members and members can meet.

decisions.name: Start from events
decisions.line: Everyone starts with events in the cities they choose. Hosting, open messaging and the wider community come with membership.

decisions.name: Contact on your terms
decisions.line: Each member sets what kinds of contact they accept. A first message also needs a path: a mutual like, a shared board or a vouch.

decisions.name: Trust is earned
decisions.line: Everyone moves up a visible ladder, from guest to trial member to member, with a stated reason at each step. Vouches from people you've actually met open the most trusted events, and there's no single trust score to farm.

decisions.name: Money never buys around the rules
decisions.line: Blocks, contact rules, discretion tools and seeing who liked you are free. Money pays for membership, never for access to other people. There are no ads on member pages, and likes, visibility and search are never for sale.

decisions.name: Rules in code, not in the screens
decisions.line: The safety and privacy rules live in tested code on the server, not in the screens, so the interface can't skip them.

rules.name: Your cities only
rules.line: The calendar shows events only in the cities you follow, and guests can follow cities before joining.

rules.name: One person, three views
rules.line: One person can have a card, a profile and a personal room: three views of the same person, each optional. Filters for faces, contact intents, cities and distance decide who appears in the stack.

rules.name: Visibility
rules.line: Everyone chooses how visible they are: sealed, careful or open.

rules.name: Photos
rules.line: Explicit photos stay blurred until the person looking chooses to see them.

rules.name: Blocks
rules.line: A block hides both people from each other everywhere: cards, rooms, events and messages.

rules.name: Inbox
rules.line: Messages are text only, with no photos or link previews, and sending is paced.

rules.name: Notifications
rules.line: A notification says that something happened. It never includes the message itself.

rules.name: Quick exit
rules.line: One tap takes you away to a neutral page.

rules.name: Deleting
rules.line: Deleting your account is one confirmed action, and it removes everything.

nether.refuses: I left out the photo-and-distance first impression, and kept each screen to a few clear choices. The interface stays calm, in three looks, Classic, Pride and Edge, each in three intensities. Meaning is written out, so it never depends on colour or an icon alone.
engineering: The app is TypeScript on Next.js (App Router) and React 19. Data is in PostgreSQL, accessed through Drizzle. Sign-in is a magic link via Better Auth, and the rate limits are stored in the database.

The rule modules decide who may take part, when a message is allowed, when a photo stays blurred, how one member can vouch for another, who is in a private group, and which pages a search engine may list.
Themes are applied in the browser: colour and intensity tokens, and icons drawn as strokes. I test the looks and intensities with Playwright and axe against WCAG 2.2 AA, plus contrast unit tests.
Search engines are kept out unless a page is explicitly allowed, and an image file is not sent until the viewer is allowed to see it.
Automated tests cover the safety rules, and an accessibility scan runs on about 20 pages.
nether.result: In testing, not launched. Before launch: EU hosting, file storage on Cloudflare R2, a mail provider, payment for membership, a privacy law review and a manual screen-reader pass. I'm also exploring a link with my planning platform, so hosts can plan an event's run-of-show, tasks, venue and budget there, while invitations, addresses and attendees stay in Nether.

stances.line: The foundation everything else rests on. Writing React, PHP and SQL from a blank file, reading a codebase I didn't write, debugging in the browser and the terminal, setting up servers on Linux, and auditing a page for SEO by eye. If every tool went down tomorrow, the work would still get done.

stances.name: Assisted
stances.line: An assistant drafts, I decide what is correct and what ships, and I review its work the way I'd review a colleague's pull request.

stances.name: Set to run
stances.line: Some work can run on its own once the limits are clear: what the model may draft, what a person must approve, which numbers must trace to a source, and what may never move between client accounts. Built well, that is faster than doing it by hand. An open chat window is not that.

moments.name: Thrown in at the deep end
moments.line: At Suntarbetsliv I took over a legacy WordPress build at short notice, with barely any handover and a tight deadline. I took the reins, worked in small, fast steps checked against the client and the users, and we met the deadline.

moments.name: The users were a phone call away
moments.line: I moved into development at Muntra from customer success, so I knew the people using what I built. When something was unclear, I could just ask them.

moments.name: Trusted with the company
moments.line: Four months into the job at Bright Swimwear, the founder went on holiday and left me running the company. I was acting CEO for a month.

moments.name: From cadet to leader
moments.line: In the air-defence youth section I went from taking the leadership course to leading the other cadets, with some lighter instructing. That was worth a lot during conscription, and still is in the Home Guard.

moments.name: Fixing stuff, literally
moments.line: “I develop & fix stuff” isn't only about code. Before software was my job, and for a while alongside it, I repaired phones at Teknikmagasinet.

quests.name: Self-hosting
quests.line: A Linux box at home running my own services. Mostly an excuse to break things and fix them.

quests.name: Travel
quests.line: I enjoy the planning as much as the trip: routes, dates and all the moving pieces.

quests.name: Events
quests.line: From a birthday party at home to a day or more with several activities. I do the research and the plan, coordinate the people and teams involved, and sort it out when something goes wrong.

quests.name: Stat grinding
quests.line: Gym and strength training, running, and a little bouldering. STR, DEX and CON don't level themselves.

quests.name: Games, board games and TTRPGs
quests.line: Player and game master. Running a session is a lot like running a meeting: prepare well, keep it moving, read the room.

quests.name: Own projects
quests.line: Nether, a community app built around local events, and a planning platform, starting with trips. Both mine, both in progress.

training: Decision and Risk Analysis, University of Gävle, 2020
backstory: Teenage years in Young Pilots and the air-defence youth section. A first job in the kitchen at McDonald's, then a young swimwear brand where selling on social media turned into running the operations. After upper secondary school, eleven months as an army ranger in Karlsborg.

Back from the regiment in 2020, after a few months in retail, I got serious about teaching myself to code. Joined Muntra in customer success, picked up more and more development tasks, and studied React every evening as soon as I got home, to keep up with them. By the summer of 2021 I was a developer.

Then four years as a consultant at Kumpan, with an AI study tool I co-founded on the side, and now SEO and development at Emax Media. The studying never really stopped: right now it's Japanese, and evenings go to my own projects, a community app, a planning platform and a plugin of AI skills I use across them.
